title: Chitreswari Kali Temple
description: This old Kali temple near Chitpur Road has a story I only heard from my grandmother: dacoits are said to have prayed here before setting out on their raids.

title: Chitpur's jatra offices and instrument makers
description: Walk the stretch near Rabindra Sarani and you still see jatra company boards, harmonium repairers and old music publishers, the last of the para that gave Bengali theatre its stage.

title: Cossipore Udyanbati
description: A peaceful garden house behind a busy road. Sri Ramakrishna spent his last months here in 1886, and the place still feels quieter than anywhere else in Kashipur.

title: Gun & Shell Factory gates, Cossipore
description: Most of us pass the long walls without a thought, but this ordnance factory has been running since 1801, one of the oldest in India. The old gate is worth a look.

title: Kumartuli's inner workshop lanes
description: Skip the main road and turn into the narrow lanes. Bamboo frames, straw bodies and half-finished clay faces line both sides, and the artisans don't mind if you watch.

title: The nishiddho pallir mati ritual
description: Few people know that before a Durga idol is made, a handful of soil is collected from outside a sex worker's home. It is a quiet reminder that everyone belongs before the goddess.

title: Ahiritola Ghat
description: Early morning is the time to come. People bathe, priests set up, boats drift past, and you get a sense of how old this stretch of the Hooghly really is.

title: The milkmen's para
description: Ahiritola literally means the settlement of the Ahirs, the cattle-herders who supplied milk to early Calcutta. A few old dairy shops around the ghat road still carry the name.

title: Shobhabazar Rajbari
description: The courtyard where Raja Nabakrishna Deb hosted Robert Clive after Plassey is still there, and the Durga Puja has not missed a year since 1757.

title: Bonedi bari Puja at Shobhabazar
description: If you want to see Durga Puja the old way, with no theme pandal and no lights, come to the thakurdalans of Shobhabazar during the festival. The rituals have barely changed in two centuries.

title: Burrabazar before sunrise
description: Get here by five in the morning. Handcarts, sacks, tea stalls and traders speaking every Indian language, all before the rest of the city has woken up.

title: Burrabazar's old trading houses
description: Look above the shop signs. The upper floors of these buildings are the original merchant houses that made Burrabazar India's biggest wholesale market long before the British were done building Calcutta.

title: Rani Rashmoni's Janbazar Rajbari
description: Tucked behind the traffic on S.N. Banerjee Road is the mansion of the woman who built Dakshineswar and took on the British over fishing rights on the Hooghly.

title: Durga Puja at the Rashmoni house
description: The Janbazar Rajbari still holds its family Durga Puja the way Rani Rashmoni started it, and outsiders are welcome to walk in during the festival days.

title: Jorasanko Thakurbari
description: Everyone knows Tagore was born here, but fewer people wander the back rooms and verandahs where Abanindranath painted and the whole family rehearsed plays.

title: Rabindra Bharati's evening rehearsals
description: On weekday evenings the music and dance students of Rabindra Bharati University practise in the Thakurbari grounds. Sit on the steps and you get a free concert.

title: South Park Street Cemetery
description: Just off the busiest road in the city is a walled garden of enormous eighteenth-century tombs. Park Street was once called Burial Ground Road because of this place.

title: Trincas on a live-music night
description: It was the heart of India's jazz scene in the sixties and it still has a band most nights. Order the old Continental dishes and you are back in that Park Street.

title: Tiretta Bazaar Chinese breakfast
description: Come before seven. Steamed buns, pork dumplings, fish-ball soup sold from baskets on the pavement, and by eight it is all gone.

title: The Chinese temples of old Chinatown
description: Behind the breakfast market are small temples like Sea Ip and Toong On, left by the sailors and carpenters who settled here and made India's first Chinatown.

title: Park Circus Maidan
description: The big open ground and the circular crossing are where the Great National Circus once pitched its tents, which is how the whole para got its name.

title: Park Circus's biryani stretch
description: From Zeeshan to the small dhabas near the seven-point crossing, this is where most of my friends come for biryani after ten at night, especially during Eid.

title: Mother House on AJC Bose Road
description: The Missionaries of Charity headquarters is just a grey building with a small sign, but Mother Teresa's tomb is inside and anyone can walk in quietly.

title: Entally Market
description: One of the old municipal market buildings that most people only know from the bus stop. Inside it is still a proper neighbourhood bazaar for fish, vegetables and flowers.

title: New Market's clock tower
description: Built in 1874 for Europeans only, this Gothic red-brick market has burned twice and still stands. Look up at the clock tower before you go in.

title: Christmas shopping at Nahoum's
description: Every December the queue outside Nahoum's Jewish bakery inside New Market goes around the corner for fruit cake. It has been the city's Christmas ritual for over a century.

title: Fairlawn Hotel
description: A green-painted colonial hotel from 1936 that hosted everyone from film crews to the Hippie Trail backpackers. The verandah bar feels like a different decade.

title: Indian Museum
description: Founded in 1814, it is the oldest museum in India. The Egyptian mummy and the Bharhut railings are worth the ticket, and the courtyard is a good place to escape the street.

title: Magen David Synagogue
description: I had walked past the red-brick spire on Canning Street a hundred times before I realised it was a synagogue, and one of the most beautiful buildings in the city.

title: Beth El Synagogue
description: A quieter synagogue a few lanes from Magen David, kept up by the same Muslim caretaker families for generations. Ask at the gate and they will show you in.

title: Armenian Church of the Holy Nazareth
description: The oldest church in Kolkata, consecrated in 1724, built by a community that was trading here before the British arrived. The graveyard has stones older than the city.

title: Armenian Street's spice and paper wholesalers
description: The lane that runs past the church is still a trading street, only now it is spices, paper and cardboard where Armenian merchants once sold silk.

title: Free School Street's book and record shops
description: If you like old paperbacks, gramophone records and things nobody else sells, the pavement shops here can keep you busy for a whole afternoon.
location: Free School Street / Mirza Ghalib Street

title: The Free School that named the street
description: The road got its name from a charity school for poor European and Anglo-Indian children in the 1700s. The street was renamed for Mirza Ghalib in 2002, but everyone still calls it Free School Street.
location: Free School Street / Mirza Ghalib Street

title: Prinsep Memorial
description: The white Palladian monument by the river was built in 1843 not for a king but for James Prinsep, the scholar who cracked the Brahmi script.

title: The riverside walk to Babughat
description: From Prinsep Ghat you can walk along the Hooghly all the way to Babughat. Go at sunset, when the Vidyasagar Setu lights up behind the boats.

title: Kolkata Police headquarters, Lalbazar
description: The red building on Lalbazar Street has been the police headquarters since the 1800s. You cannot go in, but the facade and the old gates are worth a slow walk past.

title: Radhabazar's clock and watch lane
description: A short walk from Lalbazar is a lane full of tiny shops that repair and sell wall clocks, wristwatches and spare parts. Some of the families have been here for generations.

title: Bhukailash Rajbari
description: You would not expect a grand old rajbari in the middle of Kidderpore, but the Ghosal family palace is still standing here with its twin Shiva temples.

title: Kidderpore dock road
description: The docks opened in 1892 and the road along the old dock walls still has the warehouses, the sailors' lodges and the churches of a neighbourhood that once spoke every language.

title: Sibtainabad Imambara
description: A smaller copy of Lucknow's Bara Imambara, built in 1864. Nawab Wajid Ali Shah is buried inside, and the hall is hung with his portraits and chandeliers.

title: Metiabruz garment market
description: Few people outside know that Metiabruz is one of the biggest ready-made garment hubs in India. Thousands of small tailoring units work out of homes and lanes here.

title: Garden Reach shipyard
description: The GRSE yard has been building ships since the colonial era and still builds warships for the Navy. You can see the cranes and hulls from the river road.

title: Awadhi kitchens of Garden Reach
description: The Nawab's cooks settled here in exile, and the small biryani and kebab shops along Garden Reach Road still make it the Lucknow way, potatoes and all.

title: Bosepukur Sitala Mandir
description: The small Sitala temple gives its name to one of Kolkata's most famous theme pujas, but the shrine itself is worth visiting any time of year for the neighbourhood feel.

title: Kasba Rathtala
description: The Rath Yatra fair at Rathtala has been held for as long as anyone in the para remembers, back when Kasba was a village surrounded by paddy and canals.

title: Hyderi Manzil
description: An unassuming house in Beliaghata where Gandhi spent 15 August 1947, fasting for peace while the rest of the country celebrated. It is open as a small museum.

title: Greek Cemetery, Beliaghata
description: Behind a gate on a side street is a small cemetery with Greek inscriptions, the last trace of a community most Kolkatans have never heard of.

title: Sabarna Roy Choudhury Atchala, Barisha
description: The family that once owned the villages that became Calcutta still lives in Behala, and their Durga Puja at the Atchala has been held every year since 1610.

title: Diamond Harbour Road
description: The road through Behala follows the route pilgrims once walked to Kalighat. The tram still runs along part of it, one of the last lines in the city.

title: Clive House
description: An old house behind a school in Dum Dum that is believed to be one of the oldest colonial buildings in Kolkata, possibly built over ruins older than the British.

title: Dum Dum cantonment lanes
description: The bullet that shocked the world was made here in the 1890s. The old arsenal is closed, but the barracks, churches and railway lines around it still feel like a cantonment.

title: Bow Barracks red-brick lanes
description: Three-storey red-brick blocks built for soldiers in 1918, now home to Anglo-Indian families. The balconies, the lanes and the music make it unlike anywhere else in central Kolkata.

title: Christmas at Bow Barracks
description: Every December the whole precinct strings up lights, the carols start, and the community feast spills into the lane. It is the oldest Christmas party in the city.
